problem: Before this work, language-guided navigation had no benchmark that paired open-vocabulary natural-language instructions with real imagery of unseen building-scale environments. Earlier work used synthetic or rendered images, symbolic labels in place of perception, or template or fully observable worlds (Doom, blocks world), so vision-and-language methods could not be tested on realistic embodied instruction following.
motivation: Following an instruction from what the agent sees is a visually grounded sequence-to-sequence problem, much like VQA or captioning, so recent vision-and-language methods should apply if a suitable environment and dataset exist. Real images keep the open-set visual and linguistic richness that synthetic assets turn into a closed-set problem. This makes transfer to real robots more plausible and makes success directly measurable.
key_idea: Turn the Matterport3D panoramas into an interactive navigation-graph simulator, crowd-source the Room-to-Room (R2R) instruction dataset on it, and set baselines with an attention-based LSTM seq2seq agent trained by teacher- or student-forcing.
insight: The main finding is the large generalization gap between seen and unseen environments. Student-forcing reaches 38.6% SR on val-seen but only 21.8% on val-unseen. Validation curves (Fig. training) show that unseen performance plateaus early while seen performance keeps improving despite dropout and weight decay, which suggests the learned visual groundings are specific to the training environments. Training on the agent's own action samples (student-forcing, i.e. online DAgger) beats teacher-forcing, most clearly in seen environments (27.1→38.6 SR); on unseen scenes the gain is smaller (19.6→21.8 SR, and OSR is actually slightly lower). This shows that exposure bias matters but is not the main bottleneck for generalization. The authors also report that scheduled sampling did worse than always sampling, and that reversing the instruction word order helped.
method: Matterport3D Simulator: C++/OpenGL simulator with Python bindings. It renders perspective RGB views from precomputed cube-mapped panoramas at 10,800 viewpoints in 90 scenes. The agent pose is (viewpoint, heading, elevation); actions are deterministic.

Navigation graph and action space: per-scene weighted undirected graphs built by ray-tracing between viewpoints in the meshes, dropping edges longer than 5 m, and manually fixing windows and mirrors. Reachable next viewpoints are graph neighbours inside the current view frustum. Graphs average 117 viewpoints with vertex degree 4.1.

R2R dataset: 7,189 shortest paths between (mostly) different rooms, each ≥5 m with 4–6 edges and about 10 m on average. Each path has 3 AMT instructions, giving 21,567 instructions averaging 29 words over a ~3.1k vocabulary. Splits: train 14,025 / val-seen 1,020 / val-unseen 2,349 (11 scenes) / test 4,173 (18 scenes). Evaluation uses NE, SR (<3 m), oracle SR and trajectory length.

Seq2seq agent: an LSTM encoder reads the reversed instruction (256-d word embeddings, 512 hidden units). The LSTM decoder input is a mean-pooled ImageNet ResNet-152 feature of the current view concatenated with a 32-d embedding of the previous action. Luong global 'general' attention over the encoder states gives an attentional hidden state, followed by a softmax over actions.

Model action space: 6 low-level actions: left, right, up and down (camera moves of 30°), forward (to the reachable viewpoint nearest the view centre), and stop. CNN features are pre-cached for all discretized headings and elevations.

Training: per-step cross-entropy against the next action on the ground-truth shortest path from the current pose. Two regimes are compared: teacher-forcing (follow the GT action) and student-forcing (sample from the policy, i.e. online DAgger). Optimizer is Adam with weight decay, batch size 100, dropout 0.5, greedy decoding at test. The test submission is trained on train+val.

setting.backbone: LSTM encoder-decoder with Luong attention (trained from scratch) on frozen, pre-cached ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-152 image features
setting.training_data: R2R train split (14,025 instructions, 61 scenes); the test-server submission is trained on all train + validation data. No extra or synthetic data.
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB view (640x480, 60° vertical FOV) rendered from panoramas, plus the natural-language instruction
setting.action_space: 6 discrete actions on the nav-graph: left/right/up/down camera rotation by 30°, forward to the reachable viewpoint nearest the view centre, stop (the simulator natively supports selecting any visible neighbouring viewpoint plus heading/elevation deltas)
setting.privileged: none (the nav-graph connectivity defining reachable viewpoints is part of the standard simulator)

numbers_note: SPL, nDTW and similar metrics are not reported; they were defined in later work. Training curves (validation loss, NE and SR over iterations) and the NE distribution appear only in figures. The Human result (86.4 SR, 1.61 NE, 90.2 OSR, 11.90 TL) is measured on 1,390 test instructions, a third of the test set. Human, Random and Shortest are baselines and are not listed as own-method numbers.
results: The student-forcing seq2seq agent reaches 38.6% SR (NE 6.01 m) on val-seen but only 21.8% on val-unseen and 20.4% on the test server. This beats the dataset-exploiting Random baseline (13.2% test SR, 16.3% val-unseen) and teacher-forcing (19.6% val-unseen, 27.1% val-seen). Humans reach 86.4% SR on a third of the test set, showing that the instructions are high quality and that there is a large gap for models to close.
limitations: Motion is restricted to discrete panorama viewpoints on a nav-graph (about 2.25 m apart), and the baseline agent uses a low-level 6-action space with a single 60° view instead of panoramic or neighbour-selection actions. Depth and segmentation observations are not yet supported.
Models overfit strongly to training environments and generalize poorly to unseen scenes (38.6 vs 21.8 SR). The baseline has no visual attention.

Dataset biases: Matterport scenes are mostly clean and luxurious, contain very few people or animals, and use viewpoints placed for commanding views. Evaluation checks only the endpoint (3 m threshold), not path fidelity.
